title: Team Types: Stream-Aligned, Platform, Enabling, Complicated-Subsystem

know: The four team types: stream-aligned, platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem, and what each owns.
How the product-team topology in Empowered (platform and experience teams) and the 'right team' of Build What Matters map onto them.
believe: Stream-aligned teams are the default, and every other team has to justify itself by what it does for them.
can_do: Classify a described team by type, or say that it fits none and what that usually means.
Decide whether a proposed platform, enabling or complicated-subsystem team is justified.

audience.who: Executives (CTO, CPO, VP, Director) who approve or refuse new teams, and individual contributors who want to follow the reasoning.
already_knows: How software teams work day to day.
From earlier chapters: Conway's Law, cognitive load and its limit, fracture planes, the constraint of a flow and why work waits in queues between teams.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given short descriptions of four teams, the reader assigns each a type or says it fits none, with the reason.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Classify these and justify each: (1) a team that owns checkout end to end; (2) a team of six QA engineers who test every team's releases; (3) two senior engineers who spend a quarter with each team teaching it to run its own load tests; (4) a team that maintains the route-optimization solver that needs operations-research PhDs.
acceptance_criteria.expected: (1) stream-aligned; (2) fits no type: a functional team that becomes a hand-off and a queue; (3) enabling; (4) complicated-subsystem.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states when each of the three non-stream types should not be created.
Concepts taken from a named source name the book and the concept; rules of thumb are presented as that author's rule of thumb; anything applied beyond the source is marked as the author's extension.
Each pattern in the chapter names its user and an outcome measure by which a reader could tell that it worked.

thesis.question: Which kinds of teams does an organization need, and when is each one justified?
thesis.claim: An organization needs four kinds of team: stream-aligned teams that own a flow of user value end to end, and three kinds that exist for them — platform teams that remove mechanics they would otherwise each carry, enabling teams that close a skill gap and then leave, and complicated-subsystem teams that hold knowledge too specialized to spread; each of the three is justified only when it lowers the load or the waiting of stream-aligned teams, and a team that fits none of the four, such as a functional QA or release team, adds a hand-off inside the stream.
thesis.disputed_by: The functional organization, in which teams are formed around a skill or a layer because specialists work best together and are cheaper to manage that way.
thesis.so_what: A leader asked for a new team first names its type and the stream-aligned teams it serves, and declines the request when no stream-aligned team's load or waiting would fall; an existing team that fails the test is folded into the streams it serves or turned into one of the three serving types.
thesis.how_why: A hand-off between teams is where work waits and where no one holds the whole outcome; a team aligned to a stream has no hand-off inside the stream. But one team cannot also carry infrastructure mechanics, every specialty and rare specialist knowledge, so those are taken off it by teams whose only purpose is to take them off.

supporting_claims.claim: A stream-aligned team owns one flow of user value end to end and is the default type, because a hand-off between teams is where work waits and where no one holds the whole outcome.
A platform team is justified when several stream-aligned teams carry the same mechanics and can be given them as a self-service; without both it is a queue or a platform nobody asked for.
An enabling team is justified when several stream-aligned teams lack a skill they can learn, and only while it leaves each team able to do the work without it.
A complicated-subsystem team is justified when a part needs knowledge that is rare and slow to grow and that part changes mostly apart from the streams that use it.

A team that fits none of the four types, such as a functional QA or release team, puts a hand-off and a queue inside the stream, and is folded into the streams or turned into one of the three serving types.

The four types work as one test a leader can apply to any proposed or existing team: name the type, name the stream-aligned teams it serves, and say whose load or waiting falls and how that will be measured.

role.contribution: Supplies the vocabulary of team types and the justification test that the rest of the part and Part IV's platform chapter rely on.

additional_patterns.applies_to: stream-aligned, platform-teams, enabling-teams, complicated-subsystem-teams, fits-no-type, sources-differ, name-the-type: each uses only types defined before it

flow.rationale: The reader first meets three requests for a new team that all sound reasonable, so that the types arrive as the means of deciding them. The stream-aligned team comes first because the three serving types are defined by what they take off it; defined earlier they would have nothing to serve. The three serving types follow in the order in which a growing company usually meets them, shared mechanics, then missing skills, then rare knowledge; that order is a convention and nothing breaks if two of them swap. Teams that fit no type come after all four, because 'fits none' can only be said once the four are known, and that section gives the reply to the functional organization. The comparison with the two product books comes next: its terms, experience team and platform team, can be mapped only onto types already defined, and its reading of the layer structure refers back to the functional team just defined. The pattern comes after it because the procedure uses every type, the fits-none case and the names under which a request may arrive; within it the steps for a proposed team and the questions for an existing team stand together, and the ratio follows as a check on the result of both. The worked example applies the procedure to the opening requests, and the AI section is a coda that applies the same test to a new kind of team.

hook.content: In one month of 2024 Corvane's VP Engineering received three requests for a new team: six testers to check every release, three specialists for travel-time estimation, and a second platform team for test environments. Each came with a good reason, and Corvane had no way of telling a team that would help from one that would become the next queue.

bridge.from_reader_world: Most leaders have approved a team that sounded sensible (a QA group, a tools team, an architecture team) and later found other teams waiting on it.
bridge.to_topic: Whether a new team helps depends on what kind of team it is and on what it does for the teams that deliver to users, and there are only four kinds worth having.

thesis_statement.text: An organization needs four kinds of team: stream-aligned teams that own a flow of user value end to end, and three kinds that exist for them: platform teams that remove mechanics they would otherwise each carry, enabling teams that close a skill gap and then leave, and complicated-subsystem teams that hold knowledge too specialized to spread. Each of the three is justified only when it lowers the load or the waiting of stream-aligned teams, and a team that fits none of the four adds a hand-off inside the stream.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See three reasonable requests for a new team arrive at once.
Define the stream-aligned team and say why it is the default.
Take the three serving types one by one, each with the test for when it is justified and when it should not be created.
Recognize teams that fit no type and what they do to a stream.
Map the team types of Empowered and Build What Matters onto the four.
Turn the types into a procedure for a proposed or an existing team.
Decide Corvane's three requests, and see what AI changes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In one month of 2024 three requests for a new team reached Corvane's VP Engineering, each with a good reason, and Corvane had no way to tell a team that would help from one that would become the next queue.

evidence.what: Corvane, the fictional company this book follows, 2024, 180 people, eleven product teams and a platform team of five. New ledger facts: three requests to Dario Vance in the quarter after the release-path pilot: a QA team of six, a travel-time team of three, a second platform team of four for test environments.
evidence.shows: The decision the chapter equips the reader to make, in a form most leaders have met.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An organization needs four kinds of team, one that owns a flow of user value and three that exist for it, each of the three justified only by lower load or less waiting for the first; the chapter takes them one by one and ends by deciding the three requests.

transition_in.carries_over: Three reasonable requests and no test.
transition_in.introduces: The test in one claim, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Three Requests in One Month
sections.controlling_idea: Each of Corvane's three requests answered a real problem, and without a test for what a new team does to the teams that deliver to users, the natural answer to all three was yes.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter decides: three proposed teams that cannot be told apart by how reasonable they sound.

transition_in.carries_over: The three requests named in the lead.
transition_in.introduces: Who asked, for what and why.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three requests came from different people, each with a stated reason that was true.

evidence.what: Request | Asked by | Reason given. A QA team of six testers who test every release before it goes out | two engineering managers | product teams were starting to release without a platform engineer's check, and someone independent should test. A travel-time team of three | the manager of the Scheduling team | travel-time estimation is hard, built on map data and a routing library, and distracts the team from scheduling rules. A second platform team of four for test environments | Lena Brandt, who leads the platform team | seven of the eleven product teams maintain their own scripts for setting up a test environment.
evidence.shows: Each request names a real cost; none says what the new team would do to the product teams' waiting.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane had said yes to a reasonable request once before, the platform team of 2023, and had spent 2024 removing the launch queue that followed, so Dario Vance wanted a test before three more teams.

evidence.what: Ledger: the platform team of five was created to help eleven product teams release faster, and by 2024 launches waited at it (three product teams needed it for every launch, all eleven for some; 14 open requests at the peak); lead time 4 days to 19; the 2024 release path let a team run its own release. Dario Vance, VP Engineering, joined 2023.
evidence.shows: A team created to help can become the place where work waits; the name of a team does not say which it will be.

transition_in.carries_over: Three true reasons.
transition_in.introduces: Why true reasons were not enough, given what Corvane had just lived through.

sections.heading: Stream-Aligned Teams: The Default
sections.controlling_idea: The stream-aligned team, which owns one flow of user value from idea to production, is the default type because it has no hand-off inside the stream, and the other three types exist because one team cannot carry everything a stream needs.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the type the other three are measured against and gives the reason it is the default.

flow.rationale: The definition comes first, then the reason it is the default, then its limit, which is what the serving types answer, and last the test and the picture of all four.

transition_in.carries_over: The need for a test.
transition_in.introduces: The source of the test, Team Topologies, and the first of its four types.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Team Topologies names four team types, and the first, the stream-aligned team, owns one stream, a continuous flow of work for a user or a business capability, from idea to production and for the long term.

evidence.what: Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies (2019): "A “stream” is the continuous flow of work aligned to a business domain or organizational capability." The four types named in the book: stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem.
evidence.shows: Gives the source's definition before the book's use of it; at Corvane, Scheduling and Technician App are streams.
evidence.source: Author's Kindle notes, team-topologies.pdf; author's record four-fundamental-team-topologies

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The stream-aligned team is the default because a hand-off between teams is where work waits and where no one holds the whole outcome, and a team that owns the stream end to end has no hand-off inside it.

evidence.what: Chapter 5: most lead time is waiting between teams. Chapter 1: the Two Calendars fault sat between teams. Team Topologies asks how to reduce or avoid handovers between teams in the main flow of change.
evidence.shows: The default follows from what the earlier chapters established about queues and unowned interfaces.
evidence.source: flow-and-the-constraint; the-organization-as-a-system; author's Kindle notes, team-topologies.pdf

transition_in.carries_over: End-to-end ownership of a stream.
transition_in.introduces: Why that ownership makes this type the default.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Owning a stream end to end means holding every capability the stream needs, and one team cannot hold its domain plus infrastructure mechanics, every specialty and rare specialist knowledge, which is the Overloaded Team and the reason three other types exist.

evidence.what: The capabilities a stream-aligned team needs, from Team Topologies as recorded in the author's checklist: product management, design, development, testing, user experience, security, infrastructure and operability, monitoring; with the check that a capability does not have to be a separate specialist role. Chapter 4: cognitive load has a limit.
evidence.shows: The list is long enough that the limit of chapter 4 is reached; something has to be taken off the team.
evidence.source: Author's checklist for Team Topologies (four-fundamental-team-topologies, Checklist tab); cognitive-load-and-team-boundaries

transition_in.carries_over: No hand-off inside the stream.
transition_in.introduces: The price of that: everything the stream needs has to fit in one team.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The three other types each take one kind of load off stream-aligned teams, and all three answer to the same two questions: whose load falls, and whose waiting falls.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart: 'Stream-aligned teams: each owns one flow of user value' -> 'Users'; 'Platform team' -> streams, edge 'takes off: mechanics every team repeats'; 'Enabling team' -> streams, edge 'takes off: a skill gap, then leaves'; 'Complicated-subsystem team' -> streams, edge 'takes off: rare specialist knowledge'.
evidence.shows: Only one type delivers to users; the other three point at it, each labeled with what it removes.

evidence.what: The two questions are the book's wording of the Team Topologies position that the three types exist to reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned teams; adding 'waiting' is the author's extension from chapter 5.
evidence.shows: Marks which part of the test is the source's and which is the author's.

transition_in.carries_over: A team that cannot hold everything.
transition_in.introduces: Three types that take load off it, and the test all three face.

sections.heading: Platform Teams: Mechanics Carried Once
sections.controlling_idea: A platform team carries once the mechanics that every stream-aligned team would otherwise carry itself, and is justified only when several teams repeat those mechanics and can use the platform without asking.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the first serving type and states when it is and is not justified.

transition_in.carries_over: Three serving types under one test.
transition_in.introduces: The first of them, the one most companies create first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform team owns internal services and tools, such as release pipelines, environments and monitoring, that stream-aligned teams use to do their own work, so that the mechanics are built and maintained once.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "The platform team’s knowledge is best made available via self-service capabilities via a web portal and/or programmable API". Self-service defined: a team can use it without filing a request and waiting. Corvane: the platform team holds the deployment scripts and the shared data model since 2023.
evidence.shows: What a platform team owns makes it a platform team; the source's description names self-service as the way its help reaches the teams, which is the condition the next paragraph uses.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A platform team is justified when several stream-aligned teams repeat the same mechanics and the platform can offer them self-service; it should not be created for one or two teams, ahead of any team's stated need, or when it can only work by request.

evidence.what: Do not create when: fewer than about three teams carry the mechanics (author's rule of thumb); no team has asked (The Platform Nobody Asked For); the team can only serve by ticket, which trades load for a queue (chapter 4). User: the stream-aligned teams. Outcome measures: the share of uses completed without a request to the platform team, and the stream teams' lead time. How a platform is run and judged is chapter 15's.
evidence.shows: States the condition, the three refusals and the measures, and hands the operating model to the platform chapter.

transition_in.carries_over: What a platform team owns and how it is consumed.
transition_in.introduces: When that is worth a team and when it is not.

sections.heading: Enabling Teams: A Skill Gap Closed, Then an Exit
sections.controlling_idea: An enabling team closes a skill gap in stream-aligned teams by teaching and then leaves, and is justified only when several teams lack a skill they can learn and the team's success is measured by its exit.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the second serving type and states when it is and is not justified.

transition_in.carries_over: Mechanics that can be handed to a platform.
transition_in.introduces: A load that cannot be handed over because the team has to hold it itself: a skill.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An enabling team is a few specialists in one area who work with a stream-aligned team for a limited time so that the team can afterwards do the work itself, and it owns no part of the product.

evidence.what: Team Topologies, as recorded in the author's checklist: the enabling team helps teams learn rather than taking over the work, aims at the autonomy of the teams it helps, works for a limited period, avoids becoming a permanent dependency. Corvane 2024: a platform engineer worked inside Scheduling for the first six weeks of the release-path pilot (enabling work done without an enabling team).
evidence.shows: The type is defined by its exit; Corvane's six weeks show the behavior at the smallest scale.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An enabling team is justified when several stream-aligned teams lack the same learnable skill; it should not be created to do the work for the teams, for a single team's gap, or without an end date for each engagement.

evidence.what: Do not create when: the specialists would do the work permanently (that is a functional team under another name); only one team has the gap (hire or train inside it); engagements have no end. User: the stream-aligned team being helped. Outcome measure: whether the team does the work without the enabling team a quarter after the engagement ends; the enabling team's count of completed exits. An enabling team that teams still depend on has failed (author's record).
evidence.shows: States the condition, the refusals and the measure.

transition_in.carries_over: A team defined by leaving.
transition_in.introduces: When such a team is worth creating and when it is not.

sections.heading: Complicated-Subsystem Teams: Knowledge Too Rare to Spread
sections.controlling_idea: A complicated-subsystem team owns a part that needs knowledge too rare and too slow to grow for stream-aligned teams to hold, and is justified only when that is true and the part changes mostly apart from the streams that use it.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the third serving type and states when it is and is not justified.

transition_in.carries_over: A skill that teams can learn in weeks.
transition_in.introduces: Knowledge that they cannot, and the type that holds it for them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A complicated-subsystem team owns one bounded part of the system whose safe change needs specialist knowledge that is hard to find or grow, so that the stream-aligned teams using that part do not have to hold it.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "The goal of this team is to reduce the cognitive load of stream-aligned teams working on systems that include or use the complicated subsystem." The notes add that the expertise is typically hard to find or grow. Examples recorded in the author's checklist: a video processing engine, a mathematical model, a financial reconciliation engine.
evidence.shows: The type is defined by the rarity of the knowledge, not by how hard or unpleasant the code is.
evidence.source: Author's Kindle notes, team-topologies.pdf; author's checklist for Team Topologies

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A complicated-subsystem team is justified when the knowledge is rare and slow to grow and most changes to the part do not need a stream team; it should not be created for code that is merely unfamiliar, for knowledge an engineer learns on the job, or where most changes would cross the new line.

evidence.what: Rarity is the source's condition. The second condition, counting how many changes would need both teams, is the author's extension, using the count of crossing changes from chapter 4. Every such team adds a hand-off, so the number stays small. User: the stream-aligned teams that use the subsystem. Outcome measures: the share of their changes that need the subsystem team, and how long those wait.
evidence.shows: States the two conditions, the refusals and the measures, and marks the extension.
evidence.source: cognitive-load-and-team-boundaries; author's record four-fundamental-team-topologies; author's judgement

transition_in.carries_over: Rare knowledge held by one team.
transition_in.introduces: When that is worth a hand-off and when it is not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Side by side, the three serving types differ in what they take off the stream-aligned teams, and share the form of their test: a condition, a refusal and a measure.

evidence.what: Type | Takes off the stream-aligned teams | Justified when | Do not create it when | Outcome measure. Platform | mechanics every team repeats | several teams repeat them and can be served self-service | one or two teams need it, no team asked, or it can only work by request | uses without a request; stream teams' lead time. Enabling | a skill gap | several teams lack a skill they can learn | it would do the work for them, one team has the gap, or engagements have no end | teams doing the work alone a quarter after the exit. Complicated-subsystem | rare specialist knowledge | the knowledge is rare and slow to grow, and the part changes mostly by itself | the code is only unfamiliar, the knowledge is learned on the job, or most changes cross the line | share of stream changes that need the team, and their wait.
evidence.shows: Collects the three tests in one place the reader can return to; rows restate the three sections and add nothing new.

transition_in.carries_over: Three types, each with its own section.
transition_in.introduces: The three tests in one table.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: Teams That Fit No Type
sections.controlling_idea: A team that fits none of the four types, most often a functional team formed around one skill, puts a hand-off and a queue inside every stream it touches, and its usual remedy is to fold it into the streams or turn it into a serving type.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what fitting no type means and answers the functional organization, the position the thesis is disputed by.

transition_in.carries_over: Four types, each with a purpose.
transition_in.introduces: Teams that are none of them, and what they do to a stream.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A functional team, such as a QA team that tests every release or a release team that ships every change, does part of every stream's work, so each stream gets a hand-off and all of them share one queue: the Review Bottleneck.

evidence.what: Definition: a functional team is formed around one skill or one step (testing, releasing, operations, database). Unlike a platform it does the work itself each time; unlike an enabling team it never leaves; unlike a complicated-subsystem team its knowledge is not rare. The author's checklist of Team Topologies: testing, QA, database, architecture and operations work are not isolated as mandatory hand-off stages. Failure pattern: The Review Bottleneck.
evidence.shows: Distinguishes the functional team from each serving type by one feature, which is what the reader needs to classify a described team.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The functional organization's case, that specialists work best together and are cheaper to manage that way, is right about the craft and wrong about where its cost falls: the saving shows in the function's budget and the waiting shows in every stream.

evidence.what: Larson, An Elegant Puzzle: centralized groups either become rigid gatekeepers or become advisory, with a focus on educating; the advisory kind is an enabling team in this chapter's terms (author's reading). The craft's home can be a community of practice across stream teams (author's record communities-of-practice-and-chapters). Condition where the functional form holds (author's judgement): a specialty needed so seldom, such as a yearly security audit, that no stream could keep a specialist busy and little work waits.
evidence.shows: Concedes what the functional view gets right, says where the cost goes, and names the condition under which it does not apply.
evidence.source: Author's Kindle notes, elegant-puzzle.pdf; author's record communities-of-practice-and-chapters

transition_in.carries_over: The hand-off a functional team adds.
transition_in.introduces: The best argument for such teams, and the reply.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Other teams that fit no type are usually one of five kinds, and each has a usual fate: fold into the streams or convert to a serving type.

evidence.what: Team as found | What it usually means | What to do. QA or release team | a step of every stream done elsewhere | fold testers and release work into the streams; keep a few as an enabling team. Operations or support team for all systems | production responsibility moved away from the builders | align support to streams; move shared mechanics to a platform. Infrastructure team working by ticket | a platform team by what it owns, reached through a queue | replace the tickets with self-service. Component team (defined: owns a technical part because the architecture diagram has a box there) | a boundary drawn by technology | dissolve into streams, or convert to platform or complicated-subsystem if it passes that test. Architecture team that approves designs | a gate | part-time enabling. Source: the conversions in Team Topologies as recorded in the author's checklist.
evidence.shows: Tells the reader what 'fits none' usually means for the cases they will meet, with the source's conversions.
evidence.source: Author's checklist for Team Topologies (Converting Existing Team Types)

transition_in.carries_over: The functional team as the main case.
transition_in.introduces: The other common cases and the usual remedy for each.

sections.heading: Where the Sources Differ: Two Types, Four Types, Six Structures
sections.controlling_idea: Empowered and Build What Matters describe the same teams under other names and from the product side, and where they differ from Team Topologies the four types are the finer instrument.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that two product-management sources arrive at the same default and the same placement of testers, and maps their names onto the four types.

transition_in.carries_over: Four types and the teams outside them, all from one engineering source.
transition_in.introduces: Two product books that name the same teams differently.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Empowered has two team types: the experience team, which is a stream-aligned team, and the platform team, which covers what Team Topologies divides into platform and complicated-subsystem teams; it has no enabling type.

evidence.what: Cagan and Jones, Empowered (2020), the product-team topology, as summarized in the author's record team-topology: experience teams own user- and customer-facing outcomes, aligned by the most natural customer dimension, with as much end-to-end ownership as possible; platform teams provide leverage through shared services, tooling and abstraction and reduce cognitive load; platform teams are not a dumping ground. The mapping onto four types is the author's reading.
evidence.shows: A product-side source reaches the same default and the same justification for a platform; the mapping is marked as the author's.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Build What Matters offers six ways of structuring product teams, five of which are choices of stream and one of which, by technical layer, is the functional organization, and its 'right team' puts testers inside the product team.

evidence.what: Foster and Nerlikar, Build What Matters (2020), paraphrased from the author's notes: six general ways of structuring teams: by product, by feature, by technical layer, by customer segment or persona, by customer-journey stage, by performance metric. Their considerations: maximize autonomy (minimize dependencies) between teams, minimize the impact of Conway's Law on the customer experience, clear jurisdictions for product managers, the product's life-cycle stage. Their staffing rule of thumb per product team, from the author's record right-team: 5–7 developers, 1 product manager, 0.5 UX designer, 0.3 UI designer, 1–2 QA engineers.
evidence.shows: The book's own first consideration argues against the layer structure it lists, and its ratio places QA in the team; both readings are the author's.
evidence.source: Author's Kindle notes, build-what-matters.pdf; author's record right-team

transition_in.carries_over: One product book mapped onto the four types.
transition_in.introduces: A second, which starts from structures and from who is in the team, and which lists the functional organization of the previous section among its options.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The real difference is what each source optimizes, flow in Team Topologies and ownership of an outcome in the product books, and the book uses the four types to decide whether a team should exist and the product books to say what a stream-aligned team should own.

evidence.what: From the author's record team-topology: Skelton and Pais optimize for flow, Cagan for empowerment, and the two agree far more than they differ. Resolution (author's): two types cannot tell an enabling team from a functional one or a complicated subsystem from a platform, so the four types are used for the existence test; what a stream is and what its team owns is treated in Part III.
evidence.shows: States the tension and the book's resolution, as the style guide asks of this section.

transition_in.carries_over: Two mappings that mostly agree.
transition_in.introduces: Where the sources really differ, and which the book uses for what.

sections.heading: Pattern: Name the Type Before You Approve the Team
sections.controlling_idea: The four types become a procedure: for any proposed team, name its type, the stream-aligned teams it serves, the load or waiting that will fall and the measure; for any existing team, classify it, and fold or convert the ones that fit none.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the vocabulary into the decision the thesis's so-what describes.

transition_in.carries_over: Four types under several sources' names, and the teams that fit none.
transition_in.introduces: The steps that apply them to a request.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A request for a new team is answered in four steps, and the request is declined when the third has no answer.

evidence.what: Steps: (1) name the type the team claims; (2) name the stream-aligned teams it would serve; (3) say what load or what waiting falls for them, and how it will be measured; (4) say what would end the team or shrink it (the exit for an enabling team, the review date for the other two). The user of the pattern is the leader who approves teams; its outcome measures are the share of non-stream teams that can name the teams they serve and a measure, and the ratio of stream-aligned teams to others.
evidence.shows: The so-what of the thesis as a runnable procedure with a user and a measure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four questions, one for the defining feature of each type, classify a team that already exists, and a team that answers no to all four is folded into the streams it serves or converted.

evidence.what: Mermaid decision flow, top down: 'Does it own a flow of user value end to end?' yes -> 'Stream-aligned'; no -> 'Does it own tools or services that other teams use in their own work?' yes -> 'Platform'; no -> 'Does it teach teams and then leave?' yes -> 'Enabling'; no -> 'Does it hold rare knowledge of one bounded part?' yes -> 'Complicated-subsystem'; no -> 'Fits none: fold into the streams or convert'.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: AI adds a new candidate for each serving type and leaves the test unchanged; it may raise the bar a serving team has to clear.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Emerging: organizations are creating AI enablement teams, and by this chapter's test such a team is an enabling team with an exit, or it becomes a functional team that every use of AI waits on.

evidence.what: Author's observation as of November 2026, labeled Emerging. Illustration: Corvane's AI Enablement team of stage 5 (2027, 1,100 people), named in the ledger. The shared tooling for agents is a platform question and belongs to chapter 15 and to the AI platform chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: if coding agents let a stream-aligned team handle unfamiliar mechanics and neighboring specialties at lower load, fewer proposed serving teams will pass the test, while rare knowledge and shared platforms stay justified.

evidence.what: Labeled Speculative. It would be confirmed where stream-aligned teams report dropping a dependency on a specialist team after adopting agents, with no rise in incidents. Treated in team-shape-and-roles-with-ai.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The four types are less a catalog than one question asked four ways: a stream-aligned team answers it by delivering to users, and each of the other three by what it removes from the teams that do. A team's name settles nothing; Corvane's platform team was a platform by type and a functional gate by behavior, and its QA request was a gate that became an enabling team.
conclusion.so_what: The reader can answer a request for a new team with four steps instead of a judgment of how reasonable it sounds, can classify the teams they already have, and can say of each non-stream team whose load or waiting it lowers.

callback.to: The three requests that reached Dario Vance in one month of 2024.
callback.how: All three are decided, none as proposed, and the reader can say why each got the answer it did.

takeaway.content: List your teams, give each a type, and for each team that is not stream-aligned write down the teams it serves and the measure by which you would know. The checklist gives the steps.
